articles.title: Hackers' Overreliance on AI Can Result in Weaker Cyber-Attacks, Proofpoint Researcher Says
articles.context: Even in vulnerability exploitation, where AI has been found to discover and exploit flaws rapidly, AI-generated exploits often have significant weaknesses over human-based activity
articles.full_text:
For the past few years, cybercriminals have been adopting AI tools to enhance their malicious campaigns. However, one threat researcher has claimed that AI has not made any significant changes to the cyber threat landscape, and in many cases has made attacks less effective.

Based on her findings and analysis of recent campaigns where AI was used by cybercriminals, Selena Larson, principal threat researcher at Proofpoint, shared during the IRISSCON 2026 conference in Dublin, Ireland, on November 11 how AI has, in many, cases has made attacks less effective.

“We’ve all been told since 2023 that AI will make attackers better, faster and stronger. That they’ll have access to the same tools and resources as the best developers, security professionals and vulnerability researchers in the world, and will automatically become better at hacking. This is marketing nonsense, the data just doesn’t back up this assertion,” she noted.

AI “Slop” Enters the Attack Chain

While AI has enabled threat actors to increase the speed and scalability of campaigns, a number of groups have become overly reliant on these tools, leading to frequent errors – something Larson described as “AI slop.”

Proofpoint has found such errors in AI generated malware. “We frequently run into malware where the code doesn’t actually work, there’s comments which want to do one thing, but the malware is doing something completely different,” Larson said.

A similar scenario has occurred with phishing campaigns observed by Proofpoint over the past year. Larson highlighted the case of a threat actor tracked as TA4903, which specializes in business email compromise (BEC) and phishing campaigns.

Historically, the group has impersonated US government entities to target organizations across a range of sectors, using sophisticated lures.

However, Larson said that since the group started adopting AI tools in their attack chains, their lures have really gone downhill.

This is because the AI generated emails often do not match up with the subjects and attachment – sometimes leaving the body of the message blank.

In addition to AI-generated lures, the group now primarily creates phishing websites using AI coding tools. These vibe coded sites are often simplistic and take on a similar appearance in terms of colors and formatting, making them easier for targets to detect.

Larson also pointed out that the use of AI-generated phishing messages to ensure correct region-specific grammar and spelling, can even make lures less believable.

“Human beings often don’t know how to spell, they often are bad at grammar, people aren’t trying to be overly polished. So, I think that’s actually a bit of a detriment to some of these actors,” she added.

Even in vulnerability exploitation, where AI has been found to discover and exploit flaws rapidly, AI-generated exploits often have significant weaknesses over human-based activity.

Larson cited the example of the ‘BlueMoon’ exploit chain first observed in August 2026, which involved three Microsoft Chrome browser vulnerabilities chained together.

The threat actors used large language models (LLMs) to write exploits, using information given in patch release notes. However, the AI-generated exploit itself was highly flawed, often not behaving as intended and generating significant noise, making attempts easily identifiable for defenders.

No Change in Cyber Defense Priorities

Larson said it is important to emphasize that AI is a productivity tool and does not automatically increase the sophistication of threat actor campaigns.

“AI is only as good as its operator and this is, and it can lead to more sloppy mistakes,” she noted.

As a result, cyber defense remains fundamentally the same. The biggest shift is the fact that AI is making it faster and easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities that cybersecurity professionals have been aware of for a long time.

“Attacks are attacks and AI generally doesn’t really matter. Whatever you’re defending against, defense is going to remain the same,” Larson concluded.

articles.title: Phishing Rises Three Times Faster in Europe Than Globally, Proofpoint Finds
articles.context: Proofpoint found that today’s phishing threats are drive greater engagement in Europe, with European users clicking on 8
articles.full_text:
Proofpoint found that today’s phishing threats are drive greater engagement in Europe, with European users clicking on 8.3 out of every 100 delivered threat messages, compared with 2.0 globally.

Precision Cloud Attacks See Success for Attackers

At the same time, the firm found that 64% of European organizations targeted by precision cloud attacks showed evidence of successful compromise.

Speaking to the media during Proofpoint Protect London event, on November 12, Daniel Blackford, VP of threat research, said the researchers derived this finding from account-takeover telemetry, including logging attempts and follow-on actions such as creating email rules or linking apps.

“These targeted attacks use techniques such as phishing and session hijacking to gain access to specific users and accounts, highlighting their effectiveness compared with broader brute-force attacks,” Proofpoint researchers noted.

Espionage and AI Threats Reshape Europe’s Cybersecurity Landscape

European industries are facing increasingly targeted threats. Malware accounted for 21% of detected threats in the hospitality and leisure sector, nearly twice the global rate. Healthcare organizations faced a similarly concerning picture, with callback phishing increasing by 257% year over year and malware detections rising by 84%.

The report also highlighted that espionage operations are expanding across Europe, with South Asian threat actors extending their reach into Western Europe, while Russian and Chinese state-aligned groups continue to evolve their tactics.

At the same time, the growing adoption of cloud services and AI is creating new security challenges.

Proofpoint identified more than 188,000 AI-enabled applications connected through authentication and OAuth frameworks, while the proportion of European sensors affected by attacks targeting open-source AI technologies increased 4.6 times between consecutive 90-day periods.

“Up to last year, I could have said AI for attackers was still a bit too hyped up, but within the last six to eight months, we’ve really started seeing widespread adoption of coding assistants and AI usage across the vast majority of the landscape,” Blackford added.

articles.title: 18 Outdated Identity And Access Management Assumptions To Retire
articles.context: Fraudsters are finding ways to take over established, verified accounts and exploit the trust those accounts carry
articles.full_text:
getty

At its core, identity and access management helps companies control who—or what—can access their systems and data. But as businesses adopt new technologies and authentication methods, keeping that access secure without making everyday work unnecessarily difficult is becoming more complicated.

The challenge isn’t just keeping up with new security technologies; it’s recognizing when familiar practices and long-held beliefs may be creating vulnerabilities. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council discuss outdated identity and access management assumptions tech leaders should reconsider as digital identities and authentication continue to evolve.

1. Verifying Users At Sign-Up Is Enough

Retire the idea that verifying someone once at sign-up is enough. Fraudsters are finding ways to take over established, verified accounts and exploit the trust those accounts carry. A one-time “yes” shouldn’t mean lifetime trust. Verification needs to be continuous, combining device and network signals, behavioral biometrics, and risk-based orchestration to assess risk over time and ensure trust extends beyond the initial onboarding moment. - Kaarel Kotkas, Veriff

2. Strong Authentication Guarantees Identity Security

We need to retire the assumption that strong authentication alone secures identity. As machines and AI agents gain access, organizations must limit privileges, detect unauthorized changes and restore trusted identities and access policies after an attack. Identity resilience keeps businesses running and enables rapid recovery when preventive controls fail. - Robert Bobel, Cayosoft

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

3. More Login Hurdles Mean Better Security

The assumption that more complex authentication always means stronger security is a myth. Every unnecessary login, password reset or access hurdle introduces friction for users, costing organizations productivity while encouraging risky workarounds. Security that employees routinely circumvent isn’t effective security. The goal should be to make secure access the easiest path. - Fran Rosch, Imprivata

4. Only People Have Digital Identities

Retire the assumption that identities are human. Non-human identities, from service accounts to AI agents, now outnumber employees and often hold standing, overprivileged access with no clear owner. Treat every NHI as a governed identity: Assign ownership, enforce least privilege and review access continuously. - Damon Tompkins, Pathlock

5. One Workload Equals One Actor

Giving a service its own identity addressed the assumption that identities are human, but that is no longer enough. An orchestrator, several sub-agents and ordinary application code can now act from inside the same process using the same credentials. The question is not whether the caller is authenticated. It is which of the things inside it decided to make the call. - Aviv Mussinger, Kodem

6. Trust Doesn’t Need To Change With Risk

Static trust is the identity assumption leaders should kill. In e-commerce, a customer browsing from a known device may pass frictionlessly, but a $5,000 refund, new device or delivery address change should trigger stronger verification. Risk-based access adjusts authentication to context and consequence. The payoff is lower fraud without sacrificing conversion. Adaptive identity is now part of enterprise resilience. - Sumit Srivastava

7. Identity Providers Are Always Available

Retire the assumption that the identity provider is always available. If it fails, staff may be locked out of incident response, payroll or customer systems just when they are needed most. Define a separate emergency path for a few critical actions, keep it isolated and monitored, and rehearse its use and shutdown. Resilience means proving both that ordinary access stops and that recovery remains possible. Test emergency access with the primary identity service offline. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

8. Authentication Is Enough To Govern Access

The assumption technology leaders should retire is that authentication establishes durable trust. Identity and access management is becoming as much a governance discipline as a security one. Organizations need clear boundaries around what people, applications and agents are permitted to do, as well as the ability to ensure those boundaries continue to hold as conditions change. - Jay Bavisi, EC-Council

9. AI Agents Should Inherit Users’ Permissions

Retire the assumption that an agent should inherit the permissions of the person it acts for. I can delete every entry on my calendar and pull salary data from our HR system. An agent acting for me should start with zero access, with its own identity and limits, until someone deliberately decides what it may do. That way, when something breaks, we know which agent did it and who is accountable. - Linus Hakansson, Gravitee

10. Identity Management Is Solely An IT Problem

Who can access what is now a business risk decision, the same as financial controls. When a single stolen login can stop operations or expose customer data, it belongs on the leadership agenda. CEOs should know who owns identity in their company, how often access is reviewed, and how quickly it can be shut off when something goes wrong. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

11. Administrators Need Permanent Privileges

One outdated assumption is that administrators usually need standing privileges. Privileges are not always needed and are not needed for every command. Permanent admin rights or access to service accounts are exactly what attackers hunt for. Just-in-time access, granted for a specific task and expiring automatically, makes a stolen admin account worth far less. If someone holds the keys to the kingdom all the time, 24/7, “just in case,” that convenience is being paid for with risk. - Dan Sorensen, Nexus Security Advisors

12. Phone Or Video Calls Can Verify Identity

As video and voice cloning rise, tech leaders must retire the assumption that they can verify identity over the phone or through a video conference. Instead, we have to start relying increasingly on technical signals that users are the persons they claim to be unless they are standing right in front of us. - Kevin Korte, Univention

13. Knowing Who’s Acting Is Enough To Grant Access

The next access management question isn’t “who”; it’s “why.” An AI agent can be fully entitled to a resource and still be doing something it shouldn’t. Behavior is a signal, but it only shows what already happened. Intent is the purpose behind the action. Instead of asking, “Can this agent access this?” leaders should ask, “What is this agent trying to accomplish, and should that happen?” Access should not be given without understanding intent. - Sumit Dhawan, Proofpoint

14. Occasional Credential Rotation Is Enough

The main assumption to rethink is how we manage credentials. The old-school practice was to generate credentials, which were rotated occasionally or stored in a vault. That approach assumed credentials would be used only occasionally and would remain largely static. Agents require us to rethink how we authenticate and authorize activity: It needs to be on a per-use basis. That means credentials must be generated just in time and/or there must be enforcement scoped on a per-action basis. - Alex Bovee, C1

15. A Trusted Device Proves An Action Is Authorized

Leaders must retire the assumption that device or network verification signals user intent. Possessing a registered device or passing a biometric check does not guarantee a human explicitly authorized the action, especially with the rapid rise of session hijacking and AI-driven prompt injection. Cybersecurity and identity management processes must evolve to continuously verify contextual user intent at the transaction level. - Mark Brown, The Mark of Security Ltd.

16. Disabling An Employee’s Login Ends All Access

Retire the assumption that disabling an employee’s login closes all access they set up. Include service accounts and AI agents in offboarding, reassign ownership, and revoke credentials the employee could retain so you do not leave machine access under a former employee’s control. - Kayode Faturoti, Breet

17. Traditional MFA Methods Prevent Account Takeovers

Assuming traditional multifactor authentication methods like SMS codes or push notifications guarantee safety is a dangerous misconception in modern security. Adversary-in-the-middle and push-fatigue tactics routinely bypass these basic controls to capture session tokens. To truly lower account takeover risk, organizations must eliminate shared secrets entirely and transition to domain-bound, phishing-resistant standards like FIDO2 and passkeys. - Neil Lampton, TIAG

18. One Login Is Enough For An Entire Session

Retire the idea that one login proves identity for an entire session. Access should be continuously evaluated using context, device trust and behavior. Authentication is becoming an ongoing process, not a one-time checkpoint at the front door. - Michael Gargiulo, VPN.com

Proofpoint Introduces Flex to Help Customers Invest with Confidence as Security Needs Evolve

articles.full_text:
New investment model provides organizations greater flexibility to maximize long-term value from their security investments

SUNNYVALE, Calif. – October 28, 2026 – Proofpoint, Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced Proofpoint Flex, a new investment model designed to help organizations invest with confidence by making it easier to adapt their security strategy as business needs evolve.

Security priorities rarely stay the same. Organizations continuously face new threats, adopt new technologies, and respond to changing business needs. Yet security investments are often made years in advance. Proofpoint Flex helps customers protect their investment by giving them greater flexibility to evolve over time.

"Customers want confidence that the investments they make today will continue to support the business tomorrow," said Blake Sallé, Chief Revenue Officer at Proofpoint. "Proofpoint Flex gives organizations more choice in how they invest across the Proofpoint platform, helping them adapt to changing priorities while maximizing the value of their investment."

With Proofpoint Flex, qualifying customers can:

Adapt over time by reallocating eligible committed spending across Proofpoint solutions at contract anniversaries.

Adopt new capabilities faster with Flex Credits that help reduce the cost of expanding protection.

Simplify technology transitions with programs designed to reduce cost and complexity.

"As organizations continue to modernize their security programs, they want investment models that provide greater agility alongside strong protection," said Mark Thornberry, Chief Business Officer at GuidePoint Security. "Proofpoint Flex gives customers more flexibility in how they plan for future security needs, helping reduce friction as priorities shift and new technologies emerge. It's an approach that aligns well with how enterprises increasingly want to manage long-term technology investments."

"Cybersecurity strategies are constantly evolving as organizations adopt AI, address new threats, and navigate changing business priorities," said Jared Crawley, Vice President of Security Sales at SHI. "Our customers are looking for partners that can help them adapt without sacrificing the value of previous investments. Proofpoint Flex reflects that reality by providing a more flexible way for organizations to evolve their security programs over time. This resonates with our customers, and we will invest in tools and resources that help them maximize the value of these agreements and realize the full potential of their Proofpoint investment."

Proofpoint Flex is part of the company's commitment to helping customers get the most value from their security investments, today and in the future. By making it easier to evolve their protection over time, organizations can respond to changing priorities without losing momentum.

Proofpoint Flex is available immediately for qualifying enterprise customers. For more information, visit www.proofpoint.com/flex.

About Proofpoint, Inc.

Proofpoint, Inc. is a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, securing how people, data, and AI agents connect across email, cloud, and collaboration tools. Proofpoint is a trusted partner to over 80 of the Fortune 100, over 14,000 large enterprises, and millions of smaller organizations in stopping threats, preventing data loss, and building resilience across people and AI workflows. Proofpoint’s collaboration, data and AI security platform helps organizations of all sizes protect their people, defend their data, and adopt AI securely and confidently. articles.title: Proofpoint Joins Microsoft Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) Ecosystem
articles.context: October 26, 2026 New integration embeds Proofpoint’s API-based advanced email threat detection into the Microsoft security console for stronger, defense-in-depth protection...
articles.full_text:
New integration embeds Proofpoint’s API-based advanced email threat detection into the Microsoft security console for stronger, defense-in-depth protection

SUNNYVALE, Calif., October 26, 2026 – Proofpoint Inc., a global leader in human and agent cybersecurity, today announced it is joining the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Integrated Cloud Email Security (ICES) vendor ecosystem. The new integration enables Microsoft 365 customers to layer Proofpoint’s market-leading Core Email Protection API into their existing Microsoft security environment and view Proofpoint detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal.

This milestone builds on Proofpoint’s growing integration with Microsoft services and extends that interoperability into the ICES ecosystem to deliver a more unified security experience. Proofpoint’s integration with Microsoft’s native protection adds human-centric threat detection for more comprehensive, layered protection against email-based threats.

“Organizations rely on both Microsoft and Proofpoint to protect their most critical communications and data,” said Tom Corn, Executive Vice President and General Manager, Threat Protection Group at Proofpoint. “By extending Proofpoint’s interoperability across ICES, we’re delivering a more unified security experience that strengthens defense-in-depth and simplifies operations for our shared customers. This milestone reflects our commitment to joint customers worldwide.”

A Unified Security Experience for Microsoft Customers

Through the ICES integration, Microsoft customers can view Proofpoint’s API-based detections directly within the Microsoft Defender portal. This reduces friction for security operations center (SOC) teams by minimizing context switching and streamlining investigative workflows.

Key customer benefits include:

Integrated visibility: Security teams can see Proofpoint detections alongside Microsoft detections in a single console, accelerating investigations and improving response times.

Layered protection: Powered by advanced AI from Proofpoint Nexus, Proofpoint’s Core Email Protection API enhances Microsoft’s native controls with 99.999% detection efficacy, delivering true defense-in-depth against phishing, business email compromise, ransomware, and other sophisticated email-based attacks.

Operational efficiency: Streamlined workflows reduce analyst burden and enable faster, more coordinated threat response.

“Our focus is on building a cohesive defense fabric that drives real efficiency for security operations centers, anchored in Microsoft Defender,” said Oz Wilder, Partner Director for email and collaboration security, Microsoft. “The ICES ecosystem enables customers to adapt and scale with the evolving threat landscape. By integrating with Microsoft Defender, Proofpoint helps deliver a more consistent and simplified security operations experience for shared customers in Microsoft Defender.”

Partnership Momentum Accelerates

Proofpoint protects more than 1.8 million Microsoft customers worldwide, making its participation in ICES a natural evolution of the partnership and a commitment to delivering tightly integrated security experiences.

With industry-leading, human-centric threat detection and a proven record of protecting enterprise email at scale, Proofpoint brings depth and interoperability to the Microsoft security ecosystem.

For more information, please visit https://www.proofpoint.com/us/api-email-security or read our blog at https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-protection/proofpoint-joins-microsoft-defender-ices-vendor-ecosystem.

articles.title: How Proofpoint, Varonis Hope to Secure AI Data Life Cycle
articles.context: See Also: Frictionless Security: How AI is Redefining Access in Highly Regulated Industries Proofpoint, which last week announced plans to buy Varonis, primarily protects data...
articles.full_text:
Agentic AI , Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning , Data Security

How Proofpoint, Varonis Hope to Secure AI Data Life Cycle

Why AI Agents and Expanding Cloud Access Drive Demand for Unified Data Controls Michael Novinson (MichaelNovinson) • October 23, 2026

Credit Eligible

Combining Proofpoint and Varonis will help customers to protect information throughout its life cycle, from provisioning and access to active use, said Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan.

See Also: Frictionless Security: How AI is Redefining Access in Highly Regulated Industries

Proofpoint, which last week announced plans to buy Varonis, primarily protects data by monitoring human and artificial intelligence behavior and identifying activities that could lead to data loss. Meanwhile, Varonis specializes in discovering, classifying and controlling access to data at rest. Dhawan said the companies complement each other because while Proofpoint focuses on endpoint-centric protections, Varonis has capabilities for AI agents operating in cloud environments and data platforms (see: Proofpoint to Buy Data Security Stalwart Varonis for $6.3B).

"Data is what makes AI powerful, and data is what can leak if it doesn't have the right privileges," Dhawan said. "It's the two ends of the spectrum. We are protecting data when it's being used. Varonis is protecting data when it's being provisioned and accessed, and the two provide the best and the most comprehensive data security solution in the market."

In this video interview with ISMG, Dhawan also discussed:

Why AI has a growing effect on enterprise data risks;

How to create a consolidated data security platform;

Why a larger cybersecurity company is appealing to investors.

Dhawan leads Proofpoint's human-centric security strategy and growth, focusing on protecting people and data from evolving threats. He brings deep operating experience from VMware, Instart and Citrix, with a track record of scaling enterprise software businesses, go-to-market execution and transformation.

articles.title: Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan On ‘Market-Changing’ $6.3B Varonis Deal, IPO Goal
articles.context: 3 billion deal for publicly traded Varonis was announced—Dhawan said that the planned acquisition seeks to bring together complementary technologies for securing data and AI...
articles.full_text:
The planned acquisition of publicly traded data security vendor Varonis will enable Proofpoint partners to deliver a ‘comprehensive data security solution to their customers,’ which is primed for combating AI and agentic risk, Dhawan tells CRN.

Amid the surging adoption of AI agents, Proofpoint’s “market-changing” deal to acquire Varonis is aimed squarely at helping partners and customers to protect the data those agents can access, Proofpoint CEO Sumit Dhawan told CRN.

In an interview Friday—a day after Proofpoint’s $6.3 billion deal for publicly traded Varonis was announced—Dhawan said that the planned acquisition seeks to bring together complementary technologies for securing data and AI agents, while giving partners an even more strategic role with their customers.

[Related: 5 Things To Know On Proofpoint’s $6.3B Acquisition Of Varonis]

The deal ultimately is positioned to enable Proofpoint partners to deliver customers a broader data security platform that is primed for combating AI and agentic risk, he said.

With the combined Proofpoint-Varonis platform that is envisioned, partners will be enabled to “take a comprehensive data security solution to their customers—becoming more strategic, providing more value-added services,” Dhawan said. “And No. 2, they now can work with a single [data security] provider with a larger business.”

The combination of Varonis with Proofpoint, which was itself publicly traded until its acquisition by private equity firm Thoma Bravo in 2021, is also poised to strengthen Proofpoint’s positioning for an initial public offering, Dhawan told CRN.

“We think it’s going to be even more attractive to public investors, and our goal would be to assess that after close,” he said.

The combined company would have more than 8,000 employees with annual recurring revenue (ARR) of more than $3 billion, according to figures disclosed by the companies.

Upon completion of the combination of the two vendors, “it’s a top-five cybersecurity company with healthy growth—and more importantly, [providing] the next frontier of protection, which is data,” Dhawan said.

What follows is more of CRN’s interview with Dhawan.

What does this deal mean for the industry and the channel?

It’s a game-changing moment—just bringing together Varonis and Proofpoint makes us the [premier] data security solution in the market, especially in the world of AI. So we’re very excited.

It sounds like the ultimate plan is for this to be a combined solution from the two companies, as opposed to being Varonis operating independently of Proofpoint?

[Varonis CEO] Yaki [Faitelson] and I started the conversations a while ago. And we always compare notes on the market and whatnot. [We are] largely complementary. And earlier this year, as this whole agentic era starts shaping up, we said, look, there is clearly a next frontier on cybersecurity emerging, which is data. AI is attacking data from outside, and AI is attacking data [from] inside. And data protection needs to be done holistically. That was the vision that brought us together—to say, not just that we can have one house that will be able to serve all the portfolio. But if you’re really providing data protection, it needs to be done with machine speed. And machine-speed level of protection, in the world of AI, means integrations of our signals and control points. And that’s what our vision is. We believe we can accomplish that very, very quickly, based on just how complementary our technology stack is.

What are you hearing from your customers and your partners about how urgent of a need there is for something like this?

The whole conviction of ours is rooted on the principle that this is a board- and CEO-level priority. [When] you think about it, AI and cybersecurity, those are the two priorities for the board and CEOs. And they go hand-in-hand. Without data security, you can’t enable and adopt AI. So to me, that sort of is the grounding fact for the conviction that we have, on why data becomes the next frontier for cybersecurity—and why Proofpoint and Varonis becomes the only player that no other [vendor] can do, [providing] a full and comprehensive solution for protecting data in today’s AI-accelerated risks.

Can you say whether the combined company will operate entirely under the Proofpoint brand, or whether Varonis will still exist as a brand in some form?

We’re going to talk through it—we’re going to think that through. Those things get sorted out as we go. [Both companies have a] strong product, strong following in the customer base. So we don’t have any desired intent to make one change or the other. But it’s something we’ll figure out between now and close [of the deal].

As far as what Varonis brings in product capabilities, what specifically are you most excited about? And what do you think partners are going to be really excited about from Varonis?

What Proofpoint has built is sensing how people and AI behave when they’re interacting with data and each other—that’s our focus area. Intent-based protection, as we’ve always talked about, when people, AI and data come together. What Varonis has built is making sure that [businesses understand] where the data is and how it is getting protected based on privileges and usage. So these are a complementary set of signals. We are getting the signals on the intent and behavior, and they’re getting the signals at the data layer. Combining the two together gives you the right protection of data in today’s AI and machine-speed era. That’s the complementary nature of the solution. I’ve gotten so many positive feedback in less than 24 hours, and it’s all been about this—[they’ve been] waiting for [a vendor] who brings data security together. And Proofpoint and Varonis, because of the complementary nature of the solution, [can] become that company.

It sounds like some of the capabilities that Varonis has in certain areas are bringing something a bit different to your platform?

We already have data security solutions. We’re the market leader for DLP [data loss prevention]. We’re the market leader for insider risk solution. Those are complementary to the data security and access governance solution that Varonis brings. You combine them together, and now you can protect data at rest, and you can protect data in motion, as used by humans and AI. So think of it as data security at two different layers, working together, through a combination of signals and protection.

Are you saying how many employees the combined company will have?

Varonis has more than 2,500 employees [and] publicly we have said we have closer to 5,500 employees. As a combined company, it’s an at-scale company. We have publicly said that our ARR exiting midyear was closer to $2.5 billion. They have publicly said a little shy of $800 million exiting June. So you’re talking about a company of scale. It’s a top-five cybersecurity company with healthy growth—and more importantly, [providing] the next frontier of protection, which is data.

Envisioning the bringing together and combining of these two companies, you would say this is going to be very differentiated?

If you look at other top-five cybersecurity companies, none of those platforms were designed and built to do data protection. They’re [from] different eras of cybersecurity—endpoint, network. We become, together, the company that protects data from external threats as well as insiders. Both are being accelerated because of AI.

On the partner front, what should partners of both companies know about what this means?

Partners are excited. It happened to be that yesterday we had a European partner council, and our head of Europe was running that partner council when the news broke. And many of them said, “Hey, look, Varonis is one of our top partners. Proofpoint is one of our top partners. Together, you become maybe the No. 1 or No. 2 partner of ours going forward.” From a partner’s perspective, No. 1, most importantly, they can take a comprehensive data security solution to their customers—becoming more strategic, providing more value-added services. And No. 2, they now can work with a single provider with a larger business—which is what partners want, anyway.

Previously you talked about potentially going public at some point—probably it’s not something you would be looking at doing prior to closing this, but is there any update there?

Like you said, our focus is going to be on [closing the acquisition]. And we hope to go through the regulatory process and close the transaction as early as possible. And then we think that the combined company is quite attractive to the public investors. It’s an at-scale company, driving protection of one of the key pillars, just like any other major cybersecurity platforms are doing. We think it’s going to be even more attractive to public investors. And our goal would be to assess that after close.

Agents are something that so many businesses are grappling with, and it sounds like this combination is very much going to be tuned toward helping companies with that?

Exactly. There isn’t a day that goes by whereby we don’t read the news about risks that AI agents pose. Risks that AI agents pose doesn’t mean you have to slow down the adoption. It just means that you need to adopt AI with the right degree of security. What are these risks going after? You read all these stories. Eventually, the issue is that these AI agents go to data [systems], and the data is captured in so many different places. So enterprises need comprehensive solution that can both work on protecting the behavior of AI and protecting the data, regardless of where it exists. And that’s what Proofpoint and Varonis offers. It provides a solution that enables enterprises to go pick any agents of their choice. They’re not locked in. Go pick and enable access to any data of their choice. And in that environment, their data is protected, and they can adopt AI with speed.

There are so many different vendors coming out and saying they’re going to have some solution to this. But it sounds like part of the idea here is if you’re already protecting the data—as you and Varonis are—then you’re really in the best position to help with the agent problem, if the agent is ultimately trying to access data?

That’s 100-percent right. There is no use solving a sliver of the problem. These are interconnected problems—because eventually, agents have to access data. By protecting data, you extend that protection to protecting AI agents. So that’s why our solution in protecting agentic security—through an extension of protecting data—becomes even more powerful and real for customers.

Overall, what is the message for your partners out of this, and what is the major opportunity for them?

Firstly, I want to thank the partners that have really built the business for us. We couldn’t do it without them. And this is game-changing. It’s a market-changing, game-changing [deal], really helping customers together with partners. We can be their strategic advisors, a platform for protecting the next frontier of cybersecurity, which is data, and all driven because of AI.
